abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a fundamentally new analytical paradigm for real-time systems that transcends the traditional worst-case execution time (WCET) paradigm by incorporating probabilistic timing models into deterministic scheduling theory. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on single worst-case bounds, our framework establishes a multi-dimensional timing envelope that captures the distribution of execution times across different operational modes. We present the Core Scheduling Theorem (CST), which proves that under our proposed probabilistic-deadline model, system utilization can be significantly increased without compromising schedulability guarantees. The theoretical foundation is built upon novel concepts of timing covariance and execution mode correlation, enabling more precise characterization of real-time workloads. We rigorously prove that any system schedulable under traditional fixed-priority analysis is also schedulable under our framework, while additionally identifying previously unschedulable task sets that become feasible. This work fundamentally reinterprets timing analysis from a deterministic constraint satisfaction problem to a probabilistic quality-of-service optimization problem. The implications extend to mixed-criticality systems, where our paradigm naturally accommodates different assurance levels within a unified theoretical structure. This represents a paradigm shift from conservative hard bounds toward more nuanced timing guarantees that better reflect the actual operational characteristics of modern embedded real-time systems.

This paper presents improved schedulability analysis techniques for federated scheduling of parallel real-time tasks on multiprocessor platforms, significantly advancing the state-of-the-art in timing analysis for multi-core embedded systems. While existing approaches provide sufficient schedulability tests with at least 50% resource augmentation, our analysis achieves a resource augmentation bound of 41.37%, representing a substantial reduction in pessimistic resource over-provisioning. We introduce two key theoretical contributions: (1) a refined workload decomposition method that more accurately captures the execution characteristics of sequential and parallel phases in parallel tasks, and (2) a novel demand-bound function derivation that accounts for task-level parallelism constraints. The analysis is performed in the context of segment-based federated scheduling, where we prove tighter bounds on the interference between tasks through a geometric interpretation of parallel task execution. Our theoretical framework is complete and applicable to the full spectrum of parallel task models, including arbitrary deadline tasks and implicit-deadline tasks. Experimental evaluation on synthetic task sets demonstrates that our improved tests enable successful schedulability for up to 23% more task sets compared to prior art while maintaining polynomial-time computability. This work directly impacts the design of safety-critical cyber-physical systems where accurate timing analysis is essential for system certification and resource efficiency.

We present ChronOS, a novel real-time operating system architecture that fundamentally reimagines the structure of temporal isolation in embedded systems through the concept of temporal namespaces. Unlike conventional RTOS designs that enforce timing isolation through fixed-priority assignment or reservation parameters, ChronOS introduces a hierarchical temporal namespace abstraction where each application operates within its own logically isolated time-space, with cross-namespace temporal interactions explicitly mediated through negotiated timing contracts. The system architecture implements a two-level scheduling hierarchy: the outer level manages namespace-level timing budgets using proportional-share allocation, while the inner level employs application-specific scheduling within each namespace. This design enables unprecedented flexibility in composing real-time applications with heterogeneous timing requirements while maintaining formal isolation guarantees. We prove that the temporal namespace abstraction preserves temporal isolation even under adversarial workloads, a property we denote as Robust Namespace Isolation. The implementation leverages hardware-assisted time partitioning available in modern processor architectures, achieving context switch overhead below 500 nanoseconds. A comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that ChronOS successfully supports dynamic timing contract renegotiation at runtime without system-wide disruption, a capability fundamentally absent in traditional RTOS designs. This architectural paradigm shift enables a new class of cyber-physical systems where application composition and temporal reconfiguration occur as first-class runtime operations.

This paper presents TimeNet-TT, an improved Time-Triggered network protocol stack designed for in-vehicle automotive networks that significantly enhances real-time communication determinism compared to existing solutions. Building upon the Time-Triggered Architecture (TTA) paradigm, TimeNet-TT introduces three key improvements: (1) a dynamic slot allocation mechanism that reduces static bandwidth waste by up to 35% compared to static TDMA schedules while maintaining zero transmission jitter; (2) an adaptive clock synchronization protocol that achieves master-slave synchronization accuracy below 100 nanoseconds even under severe transient faults, a 3x improvement over prior TTCAN implementations; and (3) an integrated message authentication scheme that secures real-time frames with overhead below 2 microseconds per frame, addressing the growing security concerns in connected vehicles. The protocol stack is implemented on a System-on-Chip platform integrating FlexRay and Ethernet interfaces, demonstrating seamless interoperability with legacy automotive networks. Extensive evaluation in a hardware-in-the-loop testbed with realistic automotive workloads confirms that TimeNet-TT achieves bounded end-to-end latency of 127 microseconds for the highest-priority safety messages with variance below 5 nanoseconds. The system's plug-and-configure capability enables automatic topology discovery and schedule computation, reducing network configuration time by 60% compared to manual configuration processes. This work provides a practical solution for next-generation automotive architectures requiring both functional safety guarantees and adaptability to evolving communication demands.
